Temescal didn't gain a single student while six other neighborhoods did. plan.focus: The gap between a growing district and a flat Temescal school — what the students and teachers inside the weakest-index school on the table experience while six other neighborhoods gained students this cycle.
plan.why: Temescal holds the lowest school quality index (6.43) on a table of 22 neighborhoods, yet the district around it is growing 7.94%. Enrollment moved in six other neighborhoods but not here. That static number against a moving district is the story — and the named people on this slice are the ones inside it.
checks: Open with a Packet-backed fact: Temescal index 6.43, enrollment held flat at 313, or the district's 5,201 employees — not scene-setting.
Do not write as if the index score moved dramatically; it shifted from 6.51 to 6.43 but the story is the flat enrollment, not the delta.
No invented names beyond the supplied candidates: Patricia Nolan, Jun Leu, Salma Navarro.
No invented numbers, dates, or statistics beyond what the table provides.
Keep word count at or above the desk's requirement.
Use teacher quality (6.88) and funding (11,500) as contrast against Rockridge (9.09 and 15,000) — both on the table, never implied as moving.

targets.question: Patricia, you taught in Temescal for years and stayed in the neighborhood after retiring — what changed in the building between when it held steady and now, when the index sits at the bottom of the table and enrollment didn't move this cycle?
targets.basis: Retired teacher, Temescal — supplied on slice-row; positioned to speak to the school's trajectory from inside the neighborhood.

targets.question: Jun, you're a student at the Temescal school — what does it look like in the hallways and classrooms when the funding per student is 11,500 and the teacher quality index reads 6.88?
targets.basis: Student in Temescal — supplied on slice-row; direct voice on the lived experience of the weakest-index school.

targets.question: Salma, the graduation rate here is 84.66% and college-ready is 55% — what do you and your classmates talk about when you think about life after this school?
targets.basis: Student in Temescal — supplied on slice-row; speaks to the outcomes on the table.

plan.interpretation: The numbers on the table suggest a school that isn't falling — it's holding, but everything around it is rising. The district added employees, other neighborhoods gained students, and Temescal stayed exactly where it was. That's not a crisis story; it's a stillness story. The people inside that stillness — a retired teacher who chose to stay, two students who can't leave yet — are the ones who can say whether the building feels like a floor or a ceiling.
unverifiedLead: A teacher at the Temescal school mentioned offhand that class sizes feel bigger this year, but I don't have a number on the table to confirm it.
A parent at pickup said some families are looking at West Oakland schools after the enrollment gain there, but I haven't confirmed anyone who actually transferred.
plan.closeQuestion: When a neighborhood's school doesn't grow while the district around it does — and the index sits at the bottom of the table — is the school failing the neighborhood, or is the neighborhood quietly failing the school?
